## Excursions to Templo Mayor in Mexico City: choosing a historical route

[Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) lies in Mexico City's historic centre, very close to Zócalo Square and the Metropolitan Cathedral. Today you can see the foundations, stairways and walls of one of ancient Tenochtitlan's principal ritual complexes. The contrast between ancient stonework and colonial buildings shows how the Mexica capital evolved into the modern city.

**Two current Ada Tours excursions** pass this site: [Eternal Streets and Cultural Treasures](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-history-anthropology-tour/) and [Mexico City: Zócalo, Chapultepec and the Anthropology Museum](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/). Both explore history, but their stops, confirmed services and level of detail in the terms differ.

## Why visiting Templo Mayor helps you understand Mexico City

The main temple of Tenochtitlan was dedicated to two deities: Tlaloc, associated with rain and fertility, and Huitzilopochtli, the god of the sun and war. Two sanctuaries stood at its summit, and the complex was expanded repeatedly. The archaeological remains reveal successive building phases and the sacred centre's position in the ancient city.

Visitors often notice **the difference in elevation between the ancient site and the modern city**. Instead of a complete pyramid, you see exposed foundations and sections of walls. To visualise the former structure, it helps to understand the functions of the various platforms and how the space around the Zócalo changed after the Spanish conquest.

The Templo Mayor Museum houses finds connected with Tenochtitlan's ritual life. Among its best-known exhibits is the Coyolxauhqui stone disk. However, **visiting the Templo Mayor Museum** and walking beside the archaeological zone are different activities. Check whether museum admission is explicitly included on the chosen excursion. Templo Mayor appearing in an itinerary is not, by itself, evidence that a museum ticket is included.

## Two excursion options: what is different?

| Excursion | Main difference |
|---|---|
| [Eternal Streets](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-history-anthropology-tour/) | 6 hours, historic centre and Anthropology Museum |
| [Zócalo and Chapultepec](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/) | Centre, Chapultepec and museum; separate access conditions |

The first itinerary specifies **a 6-hour duration**, a morning departure window and guiding in English and Spanish. Its listed stops are the Zócalo, cathedral, Templo Mayor ruins, Palace of Fine Arts, Alameda Central and the National Museum of Anthropology. Shared transport, a certified bilingual guide, admission to the Anthropology Museum and a sightseeing tour are included. Meals, drinks, tips and personal expenses are excluded.

The second itinerary takes in the Zócalo and Templo Mayor before continuing to Chapultepec and the National Museum of Anthropology. An English-speaking guide is provided; excursion services and tickets are included according to the chosen programme. The **National Palace** can be visited only when it is open to the public. No fixed price or separate duration is confirmed in this excursion's terms, so the first programme's six hours must not be applied to it.

## The archaeological site or Mexico's broader history?

Templo Mayor is particularly valuable if you want to understand **the Aztec period and the layout of Tenochtitlan**. If archaeology is your main interest, agree in advance how much time is spent at the ruins themselves and whether the temple museum is included.

The National Museum of Anthropology offers a wider account of ancient Mesoamerican civilisations, including cultures from other parts of Mexico. Combining it with Templo Mayor lets you compare **one particular ancient city** with the broader history of pre-Columbian Mexico. They are nevertheless separate museum sites, and travelling between them takes time.

Zócalo Square and our [historical experiences in Mexico](/interests/culture-and-history/) reveal how Aztec heritage, colonial history and modern life coexist in the capital. If you want to visit the great pyramids outside the city, compare the separate [Teotihuacán excursions](/mexico/teotihuacan/). This is a different archaeological complex, with a distinct origin and urban plan.

## Practical planning

Templo Mayor is an open-air archaeological area, so weather and strong sunshine can affect the visit. Wear comfortable shoes, bring water and allow time to examine the details. The museum has its own admission and photography rules.

Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History states that the museum and archaeological zone close on Mondays. Opening hours, prices and restrictions can change. Check the relevant site for your date, especially if the museum is central to the excursion. An institution's current admission price should not automatically be treated as the Ada Tours excursion price.

## Frequently asked questions about Templo Mayor excursions

### Where is Templo Mayor?

In central Mexico City, next to Zócalo Square and the Metropolitan Cathedral. It is the remains of the principal temple of ancient Tenochtitlan.

### How do the two Ada Tours excursions differ?

Both introduce the historic centre and Anthropology Museum. The first has a confirmed six-hour duration and clearly specified inclusions. The second also highlights Chapultepec and limitations on access to the National Palace.

### Is the Templo Mayor Museum included?

Published descriptions mention visiting the ruins, but the inclusion of admission specifically to **the Templo Mayor Museum** must be checked for the chosen programme. Do not confuse it with entry to the National Museum of Anthropology.

### Can I combine Templo Mayor and the Teotihuacán pyramids on one short walk?

They are separate sites: Templo Mayor is in central Mexico City and Teotihuacán lies outside the city. It is better to allocate a separate excursion to the archaeological complex, such as [Teotihuacán and the Shrine of Guadalupe](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/).

## Teotihuacán excursions: pyramids, Guadalupe and pilgrimages

[Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) is one of central Mexico's principal archaeological sites. The Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, the broad Avenue of the Dead, the Temple of Quetzalcoatl and the remains of palace complexes reveal the design of an ancient city that flourished from the first through the seventh centuries CE. The site is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

We offer **two standalone excursions** through Teotihuacán. [Teotihuacán and the Shrine of Guadalupe](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) combines archaeology with a major religious complex. [Teotihuacán, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/) is a private pilgrimage featuring several religious and historical stops and Mass.

## What to see at Teotihuacán itself

Ancient Teotihuacán existed long before the rise of Aztec Tenochtitlan. It is therefore incorrect to describe it literally as an "Aztec city". Its modern name comes from a later tradition, while the origins and political history of the original city remain subjects of research.

The complex's central axis is **the Avenue of the Dead**, lined with monumental buildings. The Pyramid of the Sun impresses with its scale, the Pyramid of the Moon closes the northern vista, and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent is distinguished by its decorative reliefs. The size of the squares, placement of structures and surviving traces of painting are also worth examining.

Unlike a museum in the capital's centre, Teotihuacán involves a long walk **outdoors**. Distances between monuments are substantial, there are sun-exposed areas, and stairs and stone surfaces call for sturdy footwear. Do not assume that climbing a particular pyramid is allowed: access is controlled by the archaeological site's authorities and can be restricted.

## The Guadalupe Basilica excursion: archaeology and modern pilgrimage

The [Teotihuacán and Shrine of Guadalupe route](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) lasts **10 hours**. It begins at the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe, followed by Teotihuacán. The itinerary lists the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, Avenue of the Dead and principal archaeological landmarks.

Shared transport, a certified bilingual guide, admission to Teotihuacán and a visit to the shrine are included. Guiding is in English and Spanish. **Meals, drinks, tips and personal expenses are paid separately.** Confirm the stated morning departure window for your specific date and meeting point.

The format suits travellers wanting to encounter **two different periods of religious history** in one day: the sacred architecture of ancient Mesoamerica and a contemporary Catholic pilgrimage centre. Much of the day involves travel and visits, so adding several more distant sites without changing the programme would be impractical.

## A private pilgrimage via Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco

The second excursion, [Teotihuacán, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/), explores the archaeological site in more detail, including the Citadel, Temple of Quetzalcoatl, pyramids and palace areas. It then visits the shrine at Tulpetlac and the Plaza of the Three Cultures with the Church of Santiago in Tlatelolco.

This is **a private religious and historical journey**. Private transport, an English-speaking guide, tickets to the listed attractions and one Holy Mass are included. The exact duration and price must be agreed before booking.

The purpose goes beyond seeing the pyramids: travellers visit places associated with later stages of Mexican history and Catholic tradition. Tlatelolco is particularly revealing, with pre-Hispanic ruins, a colonial church and modern city buildings alongside one another. If participation in worship is important, arrange the timing of Mass and access to the religious sites before departure.

## Comparing the routes

| Your goal | Suitable excursion |
|---|---|
| Pyramids + Guadalupe | [10-hour route](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) |
| Pyramids + Mass | [Private pilgrimage](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/) |

If **archaeology** is your main interest, ask how much time each excursion allocates to Teotihuacán. The first divides the day with the Shrine of Guadalupe. The second adds Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco, so it too includes several separate stops.

For a religious focus, the important distinction is **the confirmed Mass** on the second itinerary versus the more general visit to the Guadalupe complex on the first. Visiting only the pyramids without religious stops would require separate planning; it is not automatically a third catalogue product.

Explore other historical experiences in our [Culture and History section](/interests/culture-and-history/). For a general introduction to the ancient city, see the [separate Teotihuacán guide](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/).

## Practical aspects of the journey

- **Time:** the drive from Mexico City and considerable walking distances inside the archaeological complex take up much of the day.
- **Weather:** bring water, a hat, sun protection and comfortable shoes for open areas.
- **Access:** climbing the pyramids and entering specific museum areas or structures depends on current restrictions.
- **Religious sites:** services and entry to particular rooms must be arranged according to the current schedule.

The distance and journey time can vary with the approach road and traffic. Avoid combining this full sightseeing day with a tight airport connection.

## Frequently asked questions about Teotihuacán excursions

### Can I climb the pyramids?

Access to stairways and upper platforms depends on current archaeological-site rules. Neither published Ada Tours excursion guarantees a climb to the summit.

### How do the two excursions differ?

The first is a 10-hour shared-transport tour combining Guadalupe and Teotihuacán with a bilingual guide. The second is a private journey through Teotihuacán, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco with Mass included.

### Is lunch included?

Meals are explicitly excluded on the 10-hour excursion. Lunch is not confirmed as included on the private pilgrimage, so do not assume it is provided without agreement.

### Is Teotihuacán part of Aztec Tenochtitlan?

They are different ancient cities from different periods. For the history of Tenochtitlan, see the [Templo Mayor excursion selection](/mexico/templo-mayor/); Teotihuacán represents an earlier cultural centre of Mesoamerica.

## Teotihuacán and the Basilica of Guadalupe: two eras of Mexican history in one day

This excursion from Mexico City combines [ancient Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) with the [Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/). In a single day, travellers can explore the architecture of a pre-Columbian city and see a modern religious pilgrimage destination of great importance to Mexicans.

The excursion lasts **10 hours**, with departure at approximately **8:40–9:30 a.m.** and guiding in **English and Spanish**. Shared transport, a certified bilingual guide, admission to the Teotihuacán archaeological complex and a visit to the Basilica of Guadalupe are included. **Meals, drinks, tips and personal expenses are not included.**

## The Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe

The first part of the excursion focuses on the Guadalupe religious complex, one of Mexico's most important pilgrimage sites. It is associated with devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe and the history of Catholicism in the country.

Structures from different periods stand together, including historic buildings and the modern basilica. This helps visitors see how religious architecture changed and why the site remains important to pilgrims today. During the visit, you can see the older churches in the complex and the modern worship space.

An active shrine deserves respect for worshippers: choose modest clothing and follow photography rules. On religious holidays, visitor numbers and entry arrangements may differ from the regular schedule. Keep this in mind when confirming the excursion time.

## Teotihuacán: a city that predated the Aztecs

After the shrine, the route continues to [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), northeast of Mexico City. This major urban centre developed during the first centuries CE and influenced other Mesoamerican cultures.

According to UNESCO, Teotihuacán's principal monuments include the Pyramid of the Sun, Pyramid of the Moon and Temple of the Feathered Serpent, arranged among carefully planned streets and squares. Ancient builders used geometric and symbolic principles that remain visible in the city plan.

Do not confuse the site's history with that of the Aztecs. The Aztecs arrived much later and gave it a name commonly translated as "the place where gods are born". Teotihuacán's original culture flourished long before the rise of the Aztec Empire.

## Avenue of the Dead and the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon

One of the archaeological site's central axes is **the Avenue of the Dead**. Walking along it reveals how temples, open squares and the surrounding landscape relate to one another.

**The Pyramid of the Sun** stands out for its impressive dimensions and position. **The Pyramid of the Moon** anchors the northern end of the complex. The two differ in their architecture and roles within the overall city layout.

Your guide explains the significance of the religious buildings, the city's ancient social structures and archaeological discoveries. Climbing the pyramids depends on current conservation restrictions; **the ascent must not be treated as a compulsory part of the tour**.

## Why the two stops make an interesting combination

The route demonstrates how different Mexico's religious landscapes have been across historical eras.

| Teotihuacán | Guadalupe |
|---|---|
| Pre-Hispanic heritage | Catholic tradition |
| Pyramids and squares | Churches and pilgrimage |
| Archaeological monument | Active shrine |

In one part of the journey, travellers explore a civilisation that no longer exists as an independent political system. In the other, they witness a living religious tradition. The contrast helps explain Mexico's layered history, without suggesting that the two traditions are identical.

## Journey, inclusions and preparation

The excursion occupies most of the day: in addition to walking around the sites, time is needed for transfers. Teotihuacán's open spaces can be intensely sunny, so bring water, a hat and comfortable shoes.

Expect substantial walking in the archaeological zone. If participants find long distances or uneven surfaces difficult, arrange adaptations in advance. Both sites can be visited in one day, but the guide and traffic conditions determine the exact allocation of time.

The price includes **shared**, not private, transport. Additional stops and a personal vehicle are not part of this package.

## The excursion within a longer Mexico journey

On the [12-day Viva Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/), Teotihuacán and the Basilica of Guadalupe provide an introduction to Mexico City's history before the journey moves to other regions. Allow for the return time if planning anything afterwards; avoid scheduling another major excursion immediately.

Other places in the capital, such as [Xochimilco](/mexico/xochimilco/xochimilco-south-mexico-city-tour/), offer a different experience of canals and urban neighbourhoods. That is a separate programme, not a continuation of the pyramids visit.

## Frequently asked questions about Teotihuacán and Guadalupe

### How long does the excursion last?

**10 hours**, including travel and visits to both sites. The approximate start time is between 8:40 and 9:30 a.m.

### Is admission to Teotihuacán included?

Yes. Admission to the archaeological complex is included in the published Ada Tours services.

### Which language does the guide speak?

English and Spanish. Russian-language guiding is not listed separately.

### Is lunch included?

No. Meals and drinks are expressly excluded from the price.

## Tours including the Teotihuacán and Guadalupe excursion

In one day, travellers can see two distinct chapters of central Mexico's history: the [Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/), associated with Catholic pilgrimage, and [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), an ancient city with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. This standalone excursion module is included in the [12-day Viva Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/).

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring this excursion. The distinction matters: many itineraries mention the pyramids at Teotihuacán, but not all include **the specific Teotihuacán and Shrine of Guadalupe excursion** with its sequence of stops and particular terms.

## Why this excursion is near the start of the longer journey

[Viva Mexico](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) begins with the capital. After arrival and sightseeing in the city, **day three** is devoted to Teotihuacán and Guadalupe. The route then leaves the central highlands for Oaxaca, craft villages and southern historic monuments, and later reaches [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/), cenotes and [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/).

This sequence suits travellers wishing to experience **several cultures and regions in one journey**. Teotihuacán introduces a pre-Hispanic city that flourished long before the Aztecs. The Basilica of Guadalupe reveals another period of history and a living religious tradition. The remainder of the tour extends beyond the capital rather than repeating similar Mexico City excursions.

| Part of the journey | What it adds |
|---|---|
| Mexico City and Teotihuacán | Capital, pyramids, Guadalupe |
| Oaxaca | Crafts, archaeology, cuisine |
| Yucatán | Maya cities and cenotes |
| Caribbean region | End of the multi-region trip |

This excursion occupies only one part of a longer holiday. Consider it alongside the duration of later transfers, hotel changes and your personal interest in archaeology, rather than judging the itinerary by a single photograph of a pyramid.

## How the standalone excursion relates to the 12-day tour

The [separate excursion](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) has a stated duration of **10 hours**, starts in the morning and is conducted in English or Spanish. Its own inclusions cover transport, a bilingual guide, Teotihuacán admission and a shrine visit. Meals, drinks, tips and personal expenses are listed separately.

The [Viva Mexico multi-day tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) has its own overall price, accommodation and inclusions for 12 days. Therefore, the services included in the **standalone** excursion must not be assumed to apply to every day of the tour, nor should you treat an included excursion module as an extra payment. The final terms of the chosen programme govern the booking.

Teotihuacán lies outside Mexico City and exploring the archaeological zone involves walking over exposed ground. You will see the Avenue of the Dead, Temple of the Feathered Serpent and pyramids. Altitude, sun and lengthy paths can make the walk tiring, so bring water, a hat and suitable shoes. Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) controls access to individual monuments; do not assume climbing the pyramids is permitted.

## Choosing this journey or a more pilgrimage-focused option

Viva Mexico is designed as **a broad 12-day cultural journey** with further stops in Oaxaca and the Yucatán. Guadalupe features on one day, but the programme is not built around a sequence of religious services.

For comparison, there is the [7-day Religious Journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), which includes five Masses, churches in Mexico City, Tlaxcala, Puebla and Taxco, and a separate [Teotihuacán–Tulpetlac–Tlatelolco day](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/). This is **a different excursion product** with its own route and religious stops. Visiting similar pyramids does not make the two programmes interchangeable.

Before choosing, consider how many days you want to spend travelling, whether you want a dedicated pilgrimage and which regions of Mexico matter most. Find more options in our [Mexico tour catalogue](/mexico/tour/) and [cultural and historical itineraries](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours with Teotihuacán and Guadalupe

### On which day is the excursion scheduled?

On the [12-day Viva Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/), Guadalupe and Teotihuacán are visited on day three.

### Does the excursion take all day?

The [standalone excursion](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) is listed as **10 hours**. On the multi-day tour, follow that day's sequence and the agreed overall schedule.

### Can visitors climb the pyramids?

Climbing cannot be guaranteed. INAH rules apply and access to individual structures may change. Seeing the complex and its pyramids does not imply permission to climb them.

### How does this differ from the 7-day religious tour?

Viva Mexico continues to Oaxaca and the Yucatán. The [seven-day pilgrimage](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) focuses on central Mexico's shrines and includes five Masses.

## Teotihuacán, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco: Mexican archaeology and sacred sites

The itinerary connects three distinct periods of central Mexico's history. At [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), travellers explore one of the Americas' best-known ancient cities. In Tulpetlac, they visit a shrine associated with the tradition of Our Lady of Guadalupe, while the Plaza of the Three Cultures in Tlatelolco juxtaposes pre-Hispanic ruins, a colonial church and modern architecture.

We offer **a private excursion with an English-speaking guide**, private transport, admission to the listed attractions and **one Holy Mass**. No duration in hours or separate price is stated; the stops and schedule are agreed during planning.

## Teotihuacán: Avenue of the Dead, pyramids and Temple of Quetzalcoatl

[Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) lies about 50–60 km from Mexico City and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The city became one of ancient Mesoamerica's largest centres, and its monumental structures still define the archaeological landscape.

The itinerary names the Avenue of the Dead, Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, Citadel, Temple of Quetzalcoatl, Palace of Quetzalpapálotl and Temple of the Jaguar. Each monument contributes to an understanding of the city's layout, ceremonial spaces and artistic traditions.

Pre-Hispanic frescoes and ornamental features are especially interesting. Imagery and patterns survive in some building complexes, providing evidence of the beliefs of the ancient inhabitants. Access to particular rooms depends on the archaeological site's current regulations.

**Seeing the pyramids does not mean you may climb them.** Conservation rules govern access to steps and other areas. It is more useful to arrange adequate time for walking and your guide's explanations than to assume extra activities are possible.

## Tulpetlac: a shrine and the tradition of Our Lady of Guadalupe

After the archaeological visit, the route continues to [Tulpetlac](/mexico/place/tulpetlac/). This pilgrimage stop is associated with the story of an apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe to Juan Bernardino. For participants on a religious journey, it introduces a tradition that holds a special place in the history of Catholic Mexico.

Distinguish between the site's historical description and its religious tradition: the shrine is linked to a revered account, while a visit also reveals the life of a contemporary pilgrimage complex. Prayer arrangements and access to individual shrine areas are governed by current rules.

Do not assume this excursion includes all the other Guadalupe-related shrines around Mexico City. The confirmed stop is Tulpetlac itself.

## Tlatelolco: Plaza of the Three Cultures and the Church of Santiago

The final major stage is [Tlatelolco](/mexico/place/tlatelolco/) in Mexico City. The Plaza of the Three Cultures is known for its unusual combination of ancient ruins, colonial religious buildings and modern urban architecture. Here successive periods of history stand literally side by side.

The excursion includes the Church of Santiago. The approved programme also includes **one Holy Mass during the journey**. Its precise time and arrangements must be confirmed separately: the current description does not specify the starting time or language of the service.

The square also has a complex 20th-century history. Visiting it contributes to a broader understanding of the country that goes beyond architecture. An English-speaking guide connects these different cultural periods into one coherent narrative.

## What's included and how the day works

| Stage | Main focus |
|---|---|
| Teotihuacán | Archaeological zone and pyramids |
| Tulpetlac | Pilgrimage shrine |
| Tlatelolco | Plaza of the Three Cultures and church |

Private transport, an English-speaking guide and entry tickets to the listed sites are provided for the full route. One Mass is part of the pilgrimage programme. Additional services, personal spiritual guidance or a particular language for Mass are not confirmed.

The excursion combines an open-air archaeological site and active religious institutions. For the first part, bring comfortable shoes, water and sun protection; when visiting churches, follow dress and photography rules. Opening arrangements can change during religious holidays and major events.

## How this differs from a standard Mexico City sightseeing tour

The [Zócalo, Chapultepec and Anthropology Museum tour](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/) concentrates on the capital's history and museum collections. This excursion spends much of the day outside the central neighbourhoods at Teotihuacán and Tulpetlac, before visiting Tlatelolco.

If you want a combined archaeological and pilgrimage programme, choose according to the religious stops and Mass. If central squares, museums and city walks matter more, another itinerary is better suited. Compare options in our [culture and history travel section](/interests/culture-and-history/).

## Frequently asked questions about this pilgrimage

### Is a tour of the Teotihuacán pyramids included?

Yes. The archaeological complex is a compulsory part of the itinerary, including several well-known structures.

### Is there a Holy Mass?

Yes. One Mass is included during the journey. Confirm its exact location and timing before departure.

### What language is the tour conducted in?

An English-speaking guide is confirmed. No other guiding languages are stated on the current page.

### Are admission tickets included?

Yes. Entry tickets to the listed attractions are included.

### How long does the excursion last?

No duration in hours is specified. It depends on travel between the three areas, time spent in the archaeological zone and arrangements for Mass.
